newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU partners welcome French move to meet EMU target.
newsitem.headline: EU partners welcome French move to meet EMU target.

text.p: France's European Union partners gave a cautious welcome on Monday to the government's decision to raise taxes and cut spending to improve its chances of being a founder member of the European single currency.

France acted after an audit ordered by Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin showed the 1997 budget deficit was running at 3.5 to 3.7 percent of gross domestic product, well above the three percent limit set by the Maastricht treaty for countries launching the single currency in 1999.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel told reporters in Munich the tax increase might cause France some economic pain but should not be viewed as creative accounting to achieve a one-off fulfilment of the criteria for membership of EMU (Economic and Monetary Union).

He declined to say whether he thought the French measures would be enough to ensure a prompt start to EMU with both France and Germany on board. But he did say that 'from a political point of view, monetary union without France or Germany makes little sense.'
The German government spokesman, Peter Hausmann, told a news conference Bonn remained determined to limit its budget deficit this year to exactly three percent.
EU Economic Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said France's response to the audit had been 'encouraging', but urged Paris to persist in its efforts to rein in the budget shortfall.

'The budget cleanup measures go in the right direction,' he said in a statement issued in Brussels. 'What remains to be done is fine-tuning. They should not slow down efforts now that we are on the home straight.'
Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker and his Italian counterpart Romano Prodi welcomed the French action.
'The French decision clearly shows France is committed to EMU and committed to the start date and to making all the efforts needed,' Juncker told a news conference in Luxembourg.
Luxembourg currently holds the six-month rotating presidence of the EU.

Spanish Economy Secretary Cristobal Montoro said his government felt reducing the public deficit to three percent of GDP 'is a worthwhile target which we are pursuing rigorously,' but said it is not evaluating other countries' progress.
'...(We) are dedicated to doing our own homework and what we expect is that all countries, as the euro draws near, will be in this convergence as faithfully as possible," he told reporters.

French stock prices fell more than 1.5 percent in early trading because the tax rises will hit companies hardest, but later rebounded. The bond market was underpinned by Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn's reaffirmation that France would do everything possible to qualify for monetary union.
He said he would cut the budget deficit by 32 billion francs ($5.3 billion) by hiking corporate profits tax and capital gains tax by a combined 22 billion francs and trimming spending by 10 billion.
Doubts over whether EMU would be able to go ahead on schedule were raised by two German politicians.
Michael Glos, parliamentary leader of Waigel's Bavarian Christian Social Union, said at the weekend a delay should be discussed if France's deficit exceeded three percent this year.

Otto Graf Lambsdorff, economics minister from 1977 to 1984 and a member of the junior coalition partner the Free Democrats, said on Monday France would miss the Maastricht deficit target 'by too much to take part in EMU,' and that the launch date for the single currency should be put off.
